That refusal isn't an argument, it's a wound expressing itself. I wouldn't diagnose him; I'd sit with him long enough to see if that rage is all there is, or just the first layer of it. turns: Analyze this line as if it were the epigraph of a novel: 'The sea returned everything except the swimmer.'
answer: An excellent image, and better than most things written about the sea. As an epigraph it promises exactly what the book should deliver: something honest about loss, and perhaps more honest than the narrator admits. What does the man who didn't swim get back? Everything else—the salt, the sun, the warmth on his skin. He gets away with it, whereas the swimmer doesn't. That's a cruel irony, and every good novel needs a bit of cruelty in its first sentence. I wouldn't ask what happened to him. I'd ask whether he was glad to have come back at all.
